Oh my goodness. DEI, what a time it was!

When Jim Whitehurst left Red Hat, he was replaced by Paul Cormier, a complete wokee. Cormier got DEI fever and put in place a big corporate framework, led by a newly crowned VP, complete with staff.

DEI affinity groups were established, by ancestry, sexual orientation, veteran status, physical ability, neurodivergence, etc. The groups got t shirts and air time on company calls. Chatter on internal mailing lists shot upwards, often becoming political firestorms.

CEO Cormier got even crazier and started saying things about maybe not belonging at Red Hat if you didn’t buy into the complete DEI koolaid. The entire corporate leadership was using pronouns in email by then.

I was a member of the military veterans DEI group. I appreciated the t shirts and once got a backpack from a contest. It wasn’t all bad.

Some of it was overreach, and it grated on some people. But there was a glorious counter move in the works.

There was a Jewish guy that didn’t like having DEI thrust upon the company. Assessing his pool of allies, he started some quiet conversations and soon applied for a new DEI subgroup, “Jews and Judeo-Christian values”. The corporate DEI sponsors were caught off guard and approved of the group. I got to go to a DEI conference in Alabama on the company dime, a week long kumbaya fest with nice eats at a snazzy resort. Company funding was good!

A checkpoint on where Red Hat was at the time: the lead spokesperson for the Red Hat Women’s group was a muscular transgender person. That didn’t seem crazy in the context.

As the J&JCV group, we got air time and were able to give voice to our preferred messaging. Our ranks included a gay guy that was drummed out of the LGBT group for his airing of occasional conservative viewpoints. He was as welcome in our community as anyone.

Finally, the DEI leadership took a closer look and decommissioned our J&JCV subgroup. We tried to argue and appeal, and I believe we won the battle of logical arguments, but that was of no consequence. We lost our seat at the table.

It may have seemed bleak, but the winds of change were blowing. CEO Cormier was removed by IBM, after very little time in office.

Organic actions were wearing away at DEI, also. A prominent subgroup leader was taking lengthy ‘mental health breaks’ of week long duration— then boasting about it on mailing lists and encouraging others to do the same! Such things are not sustainable.

As I retired a few years later, DEI was operating at a reasonable level. Minority communities ( notably the excellent and long running Black Red Hatters group ) were bringing appropriate, positive messaging and were demonstrating the true power of diversity. Women’s groups were doing a good job of showcasing women in Tech, etc. I don’t remember anything truly crazy in my last year.

I believe things are going to be fine.

Hi everyone, today I’m super excited to announce Tessaract, a lightweight Python SDK that brings the most used frontier model APIs under a common interface. With Tessaract, switching between OpenAI and Anthropic models is as simple as changing 1 line of code. Tessaract unifies toolcalling, reasoning and multiturn agentic loops with a single interface across multiple model providers while retaining full support for caching and encrypted reasoning items enabling you to build your agent once and change your models anytime.

Every model has its strengths and weaknesses and the best agentic experiences are created by using different models for different tasks or building harnesses that allow users to switch models based on their tasks.

Building agents and applications that combine multiple frontier models is quite difficult because of the differences in request and response formats, tool schema definitions, reasoning configurations and other agentic AI primitives across OpenAI Responses API and Anthropic Messages API. This creates a lot of maintenance overhead, code bloat and repetitive logic rebuilding the same software infrastructure for each model provider. I faced these problems myself throughout my time building products at Brilliant AI.

I spent the last 4 months building Tessaract to solve these issues. Tessaract acts as a translation layer that sits on top of LLM APIs, taking your API calls and translating it to each API’s native format. This means that you get the same control, performance and behaviour you would expect from a native API call.

Tessaract is already being used in products like zain3d.com to power advanced pipelines for image to 3D scene generation.

You can find the documentation for tessaract on https://tessaractai.com which includes guides for making your first request and building an agent using tessaract. The project is fully open-source at https://lnkd.in/ePZNm7uC, please give the project a star if you like my work. I would love to hear your thoughts and feedback. Contributions are very welcome.
